However, existing frameworks fail to adequately address a widespread issue - the assessment of cybersecurity in Industrial Control Systems (ICS). To bridge this gap, a new framework called ICS-CTM2 has been developed. By modifying the existing Controlled Language Model (CLM) based on the Cobit 5.1.1 structure, ICS-CTM2 integrates the ICS-specific requirements from the ISA-99 and IEC 62441 standards into the framework. This model provides a comprehensive Maturity Model that facilitates a thorough evaluation of an organization's cybersecurity within ICS domains. To achieve this goal, a comprehensive analysis of existing literature and industry standards was conducted, along with the implementation of ICS-CTM2 as an extension of the CLM and the evaluation of its application as an evaluation framework for ICS.

In a competitive environment, a training agent must maximize its rewards without being influenced by external effects such as other agents' financial gains or overall system value. However, in a collaborative setting, a positive outcome for one agent often hinges on the success of its partners, suggesting that a cooperative model should prioritize the collective financial gains of all agents. Yet, cooperation can be compromised when agents prioritize their own short-term gains over the long-term benefits of a shared success. To address this challenge, we propose a novel cooperative model within a Markovian framework that motivates each agent to collaborate by introducing a virtual reward tied to the total wealth. This approach encourages agents to collaborate for the common good and yield better outcomes. To test our model, we applied it to the classic multi-armed bandit problem and the gridworld navigation task, comparing the performance of our model against competing cooperation strategies.

Current language frameworks such as BERT and RoBERTa have been applied in numerous natural language processing tasks, yet they contain embedded biases that impact their performance. Stereotypical biases, in particular, pose a concern by influencing how the models generate text. Despite this, assessing and quantifying these biases in pre-trained frameworks is a challenging task. Our study proposes a novel method, StereoSet, to evaluate stereotypical biases and examine the effectiveness of strategies for mitigating these biases in pre-trained language models. Leveraging a range of resources, we create StereoSet, a dataset that enables the evaluation of stereotypical biases and the effectiveness of bias-regularization techniques. Our results show that, although models can be improved through training on biased data, the biases are not fully eliminated. Our method provides a dataset and evaluation framework to better understand and address stereotypical biases in pre-trained language frameworks.

This research focuses on the off-policy training of a neural network that boosts the electrical tilt angle of a power system by minimizing losses. A novel method using simulated data is created, replicating real power system data to train an electrical tilt enhancement model. The validity of the simulated data and the model is confirmed through comparisons with actual power system data. The results show that the model can be trained more efficiently with simulated data than real-world data, reducing training time by over 20%. Additionally, the model can be updated with new data without starting from scratch, significantly accelerating re-training by up to 10 times.

The 4th Run of the Large Hadron Collider, which the Large Hadron Collider beauty experiment (LHCb) participated in, marked a significant milestone in determining the CKM angle $\gamma$. The experiment, which included a variety of $\gamma$-sensitive measurements, provided valuable estimates through a fit or simulation-based approach. This study aims to offer an alternative perspective by combining results from different experiments and developing a new method to extract $\gamma$ based on its correlation with various $b\to q\bar q^*$ measurements. Utilizing multivariate regression, which takes advantage of the strengths of each individual measurement, this study yields an estimate of $\gamma$ under different scenarios. Firstly, assuming all measurements are independent, this results in a world average estimate of $\gtrsim 7^{\circ}$. Secondly, by incorporating correlations between measurements, this leads to a more precise estimate of $\gtrsim 0.9^{\circ}$. The study further demonstrates that, in the latter scenario, $\gamma$ can be determined with an error margin of less than $1^{\circ}$ using a likelihood fit.

This study focuses on a type of intricate ellipsoid known as the intricate ellipsoid, characterized by complex properties. It is demonstrated that the homeomorphism group of the intricate ellipsoid over $\mathbb{R}^n$ contains an arithmetic subgroup, which is a significant outcome with far-reaching implications. Building upon this finding, several corollaries are derived, including the existence of complicated groups, topological groups and Lie groups, all of which are derived from the intricate ellipsoid. Additionally, the intricate ellipsoid's properties lead to the discovery of new families of groups, such as the congruence subgroup series associated with the hyperbolic manifold, as well as the existence of complicated Riemann surfaces and their automorphic forms.

People's personal data is highly valued on platforms connecting data buyers and sellers, yet the complex process of sharing personal data remains poorly understood. To address this, we conducted two studies examining users' intentions to join a platform trading personal data. One study revealed that users are hesitant to share data due to safety concerns but still have positive motivations. A subsequent study, while confirming these findings, revealed users would only participate if certain conditions are met. Our research provides valuable insights guiding the development of user-friendly personal data platforms.

In 5G systems, Quicker-than-Nyquist (QTN) signaling schemes, like low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with FTN schemes, are gaining traction. FTN schemes can increase spectral efficiency, but they complicate detection due to increased computational complexity. This paper presents a deep learning-based method to identify FTN-coded LDPC-coded messages, which outperforms existing sphere decoding approaches by several orders of magnitude, even for large block lengths and excessive tail bits.

Impact algebras, a development of Fuzzy Logic, serve as an extension of classical algebras, incorporating infinite values between 0 and 1. Within the realm of impact algebras, this research explores two novel topological structures - arrangement topology and Frink ideal topology. We delve into the properties, relationships, and comparability of these topological structures, further demonstrating that a compatible topology can be derived from the pre-order impact topology. Furthermore, we establish that in finite impact algebras, arrangement and Frink ideal topologies are equivalent, yet this equivalence does not extend to an infinite impact algebra framework.

Recent studies demonstrate that utilizing segmentation maps derived from pre-trained models significantly enhances image classification accuracy through the strategic manipulation of training data exposure to edge and boundary features. This paper proposes a novel data augmentation technique, SaliencyMix, which combines original images with randomly cropped segments from other training images, thereby enhancing model performance. The proposed method outperforms traditional random cropping in several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet with superior results.

Our investigation focuses on an $SL_2$-module of the same type developed by F. H. Clarke within the infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke ring. We establish a specific shift in the Konno--Stokoe Konno--Stokoe operator's eigenvalue distribution, specifically its eigenvalue zero, which had been located at $x=1/2$ by Konno--Stokoe and later at $x=0$ by F. H. Clarke and R. Roelcke--A. Takagi through a different method. We also identify a modified trace on the infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke ring that is related to the shift in the eigenvalue distribution. We demonstrate that this trace is consistent with the trace previously defined by F. H. Clarke on the $SL_2$-module in question.

A novel method is proposed that uses gravitational lensing effects combined 
with tidal intrinsic galaxy alignments to distinguish between modified gravity 
theories and the standard Lambda-Cold-Dark-Matter model. By separating the 
lensing and alignment signal, the method is able to determine how different 
astronomical probes are affected by gravitational distortions. Using a cosmological 
simulation, the method is demonstrated to be able to accurately recover the 
parameters of the Lambda-Cold-Dark-Matter model, but fails to do so when 
modified by the axion-type dark matter model. The method is also able to rule 
out models of gravity that deviate from General Relativity at high confidence.

We investigate the flow behavior of powders composed of soft glass particles using computer simulations. The material's response to stress is studied as it is compressed between plates. The material's yield stress is found to increase with compression speed, which is a common issue in these types of systems. To understand why this happens, we analyzed how the particles are arranged and found that increasing compression speed leads to more disordered structures. We discovered that when the material is already highly disordered, applying stress to it results in a sudden and permanent change in its state, which is known as a shear jamming transition. This transition is characterized by a rapid increase in yield stress and is found to occur even at low compression speeds, which is why increasing the compression speed actually makes the transition more difficult to achieve. Our research provides new insights into the jamming transition and its relationship to the properties of the material.

A novel approach to simulating and analyzing gold nanoparticle fusion reactions is proposed. The method leverages data-driven simulations, which integrate empirical data into a physical model, allowing for a quantitative framework that bridges experimental and computational research approaches. A key characteristic of these reactions is their ability to form stable, droplet-shaped droplets, which is often modeled using the drop volume theory. However, the effectiveness of this model is constrained by its reliance on unmeasurable variables. This limitation is addressed by our approach, which uses experimental data in a way that makes the model more robust and adaptable. The method is validated through its application to data-informed simulations of fusion reactions involving 10 nm and 20 nm gold nanoparticles. The results show that incorporating experimental droplet images into the simulations enhances their accuracy. The method is also used to investigate the influence of various factors, such as the ionic strength and contact area of the particles, on the fusion process. Ultimately, this approach enables researchers to efficiently design experiments, simulate outcomes, and make quantitative predictions about the fusion behavior of nanoparticles in various conditions.

We establish parameterized division theorems for pseudodifferential operators with phase functions varying by parameters. This allows for the transformation of bifurcation and perturbation problems into problems of operator polynomial perturbations, using the resulting structure to analyze the effect of parameter changes on the original system, often without requiring the original phase functions. The resulting theorems have various applications in bifurcation analysis and bifurcation detection, and in the context of classical mechanics, can also be utilized in the derivation of generalized Umehara's Regulus Theorems.

In taste evaluation, four distinct flavors are commonly defined: sweet, bitter, sour, and salty. We suggest an alternative tetrahedral structure, based on mathematical properties, that incorporates a unique point representing complexity. This complexity, represented by the term "umami," is often regarded as a separate taste element. Our tetrahedral framework, however, demonstrates that "umami" is a derived concept resulting from combining the three fundamental tastes, much like how a point on a sphere is determined by its coordinates corresponding to two opposing vertices of an equilateral triangle.

We obtain novel closed-form expressions for (h;q)Genocchi numbers and polynomials with weights, along with their respective twisted variants. Additionally, we derive an alternative approach to defining (h;q)Genocchi polynomials, and establish new summation formulas for (h,q)-Genocchi polynomials with weights, as well as their twisted counterparts, by employing the Laplace transform, Cauchy transform, and Mehler's formula.

To address the complexity of predicting future medical conditions, 
we developed a novel method that utilizes data from electronic health records, 
incorporating both temporal patterns and hidden relationships between different health metrics. 
Our focus was on patients who suffer from diabetes and are at risk of developing diabetic retinopathy, 
a long-term complication that can be costly and cause blindness if not addressed. 
Our goal was to create a model that not only identifies patients with diabetic retinopathy, 
but also forecasts their treatment progress over the next 5 years. 
We applied a reinforcement learning approach, using a neural network model that incorporated a long short-term memory unit, 
to develop a method that could be trained using an enhanced cross-entropy method algorithm. 
Our results showed that the model was able to identify patients with diabetic retinopathy with 85.6% accuracy, 
while also detecting patients who will develop the condition with a positive predictive value of 99.3% 
and a high average net utility of 0.05. 
These results indicate that the model is highly effective in predicting the future outcomes for patients with diabetic retinopathy.

Epidemiological studies often use case-control designs to identify risk factors for disease, but participants' recall can be tainted by memory bias. In response, researchers have developed various methods to correct for the distortion, but these strategies can only account for the bias up to a point. A new approach, called causal deduction, is a probabilistic method that can quantify the likelihood of exposure causing disease. It utilizes data from case-control studies and statistical models to estimate this relationship. In contrast to traditional exposure causality models, causal deduction focuses on disease causing exposure, which is particularly advantageous in studies where the disease is rare. A key benefit of causal deduction is its ability to utilize any statistical model, regardless of whether it's causal or not. This flexibility makes it an ideal complement to other methods for identifying causal effects. Importantly, causal deduction can also be applied to scenarios where exposure precedes disease, and future disease status is unknown.

Autoencoders are a type of model that can be trained in two ways: either by directly maximizing a likelihood function based on the model parameters, or by finding a tractable lower bound of the log-likelihood and optimizing the parameters that maximize it. While the direct approach is ideal, it can be very computationally expensive, often requiring the use of inverter networks to enable training, whereas the variational approach results in an approximate maximum likelihood estimate and may lead to a loss in the accuracy of the inferred latent representations. Our research focuses on a direct approach to training generative autoencoders, specifically incorporating the concept of invertible neural networks to enable efficient and precise training of models at scale. Our experiments show that this direct approach produces high-quality, efficient, and scalable autoencoders, yielding superior results in terms of both log-likelihood and qualitative performance.

The analysis of large-scale urban data has become essential in the modern era of smart cities. Accurate and efficient data assessment plays a crucial role in enhancing decision-making processes that ultimately benefit citizens. Nevertheless, the assessment process for urban data remains a pressing concern, encompassing tasks such as data verification, validation, and comparison with other metropolitan areas. To this end, this study introduces a novel approach grounded in data mining, visualization, and user-centric design. Our proposed framework enables the identification of feature patterns in urban data, allowing for meaningful comparisons with reference data and the evaluation of a city's performance in key areas. Through our method, users can adjust the level of detail in the assessment results and leverage our visualization tool to facilitate a more user-friendly experience. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted an empirical study using real-world data from the City of Ottawa.

This paper explores various geometric multigrid techniques as preconditioners for HDG-P0 systems resulting from reaction-diffusion equations and generalized Stokes problems. Two coarsening strategies and four algebraic smoothing techniques are examined. Additionally, two optimization approaches are presented, which involve non-uniform coarse grid spacing in one direction, leading to significant cost reduction. Our numerical results confirm the efficiency of the approaches, with the optimal combinations achieving runtime reductions of over two-fold compared to standard geometric multigrid.

The vast amount of scientific literature hinders the generalization of findings to unstudied populations and outcomes. As a result, current causal evidence is limited to specific populations and is often accompanied by concerns about applicability. For instance, a finding that vitamin D supplements may alleviate fractures in European postmenopausal women does not necessarily extend to older individuals from India or to the prevention of bone fractures in men. To address this issue, we have developed a novel Bayesian framework that assesses the applicability of causal findings to missing populations. By focusing on the joint distribution of the missing populations given the observed ones, we have formulated a Bayesian metric called the Bayesian applicability ratio (BAR). Unlike previous metrics, BAR is a well-defined statistical quantity, as opposed to a distribution, and can be estimated using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. Through simulation studies, we have shown that the proposed BAR metric outperforms existing metrics in estimating the applicability ratio, even in the presence of missing data and varying prior distributions.

A common statistical analysis in crossover studies, traditionally used for binary data, has been adapted for continuous multivariate data without incorporating probability calculations. Our objective is to formulate a coherent approach for evaluating missing multivariate crossover trial data by analyzing likelihood ratios and corresponding probabilities. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been established for evaluating crossover trials with missing data from multivariate random variables. Our proposed method calculates conditional probabilities for missing observations, and estimates trial efficacy based on these probabilities. A Monte-Carlo simulation was used to assess the accuracy of estimating model parameters and efficiency in a specific scenario. Our results indicate that this probability-based method performs well in small crossover trials and accurately handles missing data.

In a recent study, the concept of a 'fragile monoidal framework' was developed, encompassing a broad category along with a monoidal structure and specific requirements. Researchers then identified a necessary condition for the existence of a coherent coherent homotopy category, in which the associated Rothe associahedra are realizable as Deligne-type stable combinations of simplicial complexes, specifically CW-complexes. Building upon this, the study demonstrates the feasibility of constructing certain fragile monoidal frameworks by using specific categories, such as stable categories of modules over a stable commutative ring and coherent sheaf cohomology. Additionally, the study outlines a method to calculate the homotopy categories of coherent cohomologies associated with these frameworks.

Memory controllers can access DRAM efficiently through a limited set of available commands.  In order to overcome this constraint, a new memory controller called CODIC was designed to allow for the execution of arbitrary commands.  CODIC achieves this by utilizing a special module in the DRAM that processes new commands.  In order to ensure compatibility with existing systems, CODIC utilizes an interface to translate user-specified commands into those recognized by the DRAM, and in some cases, CODIC modifies the DRAM's command set.  In order to evaluate the functionality of CODIC, a number of applications were implemented that utilize its capabilities.  For instance, CODIC was able to efficiently implement a cache that could be accessed externally and it improved the performance of a cache-based encryption system by 3.5 times.  Additionally, CODIC was able to efficiently implement an in-memory database system that utilized a hash index that could be updated efficiently and it improved the performance of this database system by 1.5 times.  In general, CODIC was able to efficiently process new commands and it did not negatively affect the performance of the system.

This paper delves into the use of functional programming in designing and
implementing software components for cloud-based management and orchestration
systems. We examine specific techniques for managing network resources, including
porting, configuring, and monitoring network assets. By applying a functional
approach, we provide clear definitions for assets, networks, and configurations,
while also developing efficient tools for creating and managing network assets.
A key challenge in virtualized environments involves ensuring consistent network
configurations across assets, platforms, and cloud environments. We demonstrate
how functional programming can facilitate this by providing a modular approach
to configuration management. We also discuss the benefits of using immutable data
structures for monitoring and troubleshooting purposes.

To enhance the performance of topological quantum computing devices, researchers need to create and manipulate error-correcting codes in these systems. This study investigates the feasibility of generating a high-frequency resonator's entanglement within a toric code framework, as it's crucial for enhancing quantum operations in such devices. It's found that achieving two-qubit operations on the corner qubits of a 2D code can be accomplished, but implementing similar operations on the bulk qubits is highly challenging. This disparity arises due to differences in detection efficiency between two-qubit and multi-qubit operations, which can be quantified by comparing the energy barriers separating different symmetry-protected topological phases. To validate these findings, the study proposes a set of experiments that can be performed on the superconducting platform.

The large-scale, distributed research infrastructure created by e-Research Infrastructure in Norway (ERN) requires an advanced job management system. The current system, CLARITY, restricts project access and only supports a limited number of users, making it unsuitable for a broader, distributed infrastructure. To address this issue, we propose OPUS - a comprehensive, distributed job management system that adheres to OASIS job manager standards. OPUS minimizes system complexity, enables a user-friendly interface, and allows for user authentication. We designed OPUS to accommodate a variety of resources, including render farms and computing clusters. The system will be tested with e-Research Infrastructure (ERN) providers and clients in the fall of 2021.

This study introduces an interactive learning approach that leverages game-related techniques to educate students about the complexities of IEEE-based networks. By contrast to conventional teaching methods, this research focuses on enhancing students' understanding of the process perspective of IEEE networks through hands-on training. Two case studies are presented to demonstrate the application of intrinsically and extrinsically motivated game-based learning. Data collected from a survey reveals that students appreciate the novel educational approach, leading to a potential expansion of game-based learning in the domain of comprehensive IEEE networks. Notably, this research contributes to a better understanding of the process perspective of IEEE networks by integrating the S-TG model, a theoretical framework in game-based learning studies.

The method of tracking ozone and oxygen levels in a planet's atmosphere to identify life has been widely used but may not always be reliable. This is demonstrated by the analysis of O2 and O3 mixing ratios in atmospheres composed of N2 and CO2, which showed that ozone can be generated without the presence of oxygen. Further analysis revealed that the O2-O3 relationship in these atmospheres is complex and depends on several factors, including the atmospheric CO2 concentration, altitude, and the presence of other atmospheric components. The findings suggest that the Figenbaum number, which represents the O3 maximum mixing ratio, can be used as a proxy for O2 in certain cases but is often unreliable.

In higher-dimensional quantum systems, non-equilibrium processes often occur, but their microscopic understanding is still unclear. To gain a more detailed understanding, we investigate the dynamics of non-equilibrium surface flows on a 3D quantum crystal that exhibits fractional charge properties. This study reveals both equilibrium and nonequilibrium flows with unique characteristics, including steady-state conditions and a unique response to harmonic perturbations. Furthermore, we observe a pattern of nonequilibrium surface flows with a fractal structure, similar to the fractal bands found in higher-dimensional quantum systems.

Recent advancements in multilingual neural machine translation (MNMT) have been notable, with notable improvements in translating less commonly used languages. Nevertheless, these models face difficulties generalizing to specialized domains, such as medical writing, particularly when translating languages with limited available data. To overcome these challenges, our research investigates the effectiveness of fine-tuning a multilingual neural machine translation model on targeted medical datasets and assessing the impact of domain-specific training on translation outcomes. Specifically, our study focuses on translating medical texts in Portuguese and Spanish, two languages with distinct levels of linguistic resources availability. We examine the performance of our model in translating medical texts in an unadapted setting, in Portuguese, and compare it to the performance in Spanish, which had more source language resources available. Furthermore, our results show the impact of fine-tuning on translation quality and the capacity for domain adaptation across languages.

In a plasma system comprising cold nonthermal electrons and warm ion fluid electrons, solitary and shock waves propagate at a specific speed that is influenced by the phase speed of the background waves, which in turn is determined by the parameters of the plasma. However, due to the non-elastic behavior of nonthermal electrons, the plasma's parameters do not accurately represent the wave properties. Consequently, a theoretical model has been developed to account for the non-elastic behavior of nonthermal electrons and the effects of particle fluctuations on wave properties, enabling the prediction of wave speeds and parameters, such as the fluid temperature and nonthermal electron density, which can be experimentally measured.

Recent advancements in machine learning systems have led to the development of powerful language models capable of extracting contextual and generative information from text. In this study, we demonstrate the applicability of such models to the task of dense retrieval, and introduce an unsupervised, data-to-text approach that utilizes the CLIP framework to create multilingual sentence representations. By employing this method, we are able to significantly surpass the state-of-the-art in a multilingual large-scale news dataset while minimizing the requirement for human annotation, and achieve competitive results in zero-shot cross-language document retrieval.

Multimodal learning models have excelled in various computer vision tasks, yet their performance often suffers from the presence of diverse modalities with numerous possible combinations. A primary challenge lies in balancing the influence of different modalities within a single neural network, a task that has garnered increasing attention in recent years. This issue stems from the fact that existing models typically treat all modalities as if they were equally vital, overlooking the potential for improving performance by selectively adjusting the contribution of less important modalities. In this research, we introduce a novel method called Prototypical Modal Adjustment (PMA). This innovative approach leverages prototypical samples as a distinct class representation, allowing for the identification of less vital modalities and thereby selectively adjusting their influence. Moreover, PMA features an efficient training strategy that eliminates the need for manual selection of modalities, enabling the model to effectively prioritize the most crucial modalities. We rigorously test our proposed method on a range of tasks, achieving superior results compared to existing models, particularly when modalities are scarce. We also conduct an in-depth examination of the model's behavior, illustrating its capacity to selectively prioritize the most valuable modalities.

This research expands on conveyance theory, originally developed by A. N. Balakrishnan, to create a comprehensive framework. Conveyance theory initially calculated the likelihood of a stochastic process being altered by $z$-transformed white noise, then extended this concept to consider the likelihood of any arbitrary noise process modifying a linear shift-invariant system. Building upon this foundation, we propose an enhanced framework, where specific noise processes are assigned greater weight in calculating system likelihood. This new framework is based on two distinct concepts: the first, based on the correlation between the noise process and the $z$-transform of its convolution, and the second, based on the correlation between the noise process and its own $z$-transform. By considering these two approaches, we derive a general theory of conveyance and establish the theory of frequency-engagement conveyance as a specific instance of this expanded framework, where the latter's weight is tied to frequency response characteristics. By contrast, in frequency-engagement conveyance, the weight is tied to the correlation between the noise process and its own frequency response characteristics. Finally, we demonstrate that frequency-engagement conveyance represents a particular case of the broader vector-engagement conveyance framework, where the latter's vector weight is a complex-valued function of frequency, and whose properties and implications are explored in detail.

Verbal command recognition technology has a broad-reaching impact on various fields, 
enabling autonomous devices to interact with humans in a more efficient manner.
This research explores the application of tensor-train networks in addressing 
key challenges related to verbal command recognition, particularly in 
sequence classification and data augmentation. Our findings indicate that using 
tensor-truss networks can lead to a significant reduction in the number of 
gates required to classify sequences of acoustic features, resulting in 
substantial improvements in computational efficiency. Moreover, we discovered 
that augmenting training data through forced alignment and random data 
manipulation techniques can significantly enhance the accuracy of 
tensor-truss network-based verbal command recognition models.

A novel approach to calculating the probability of specific outcomes in open quantum systems is introduced, based on an implicit method that doesn't need to explicitly expand the system's density operator. This method is applied to a three-level open quantum system with two dissipative channels, and the resulting numerical analysis provides exact probabilities for transitions between the system's internal states. An example shows that the collapse of a coherent state in a system affected by both dissipation and spontaneous emission results in a combination of direct and multi-step transitions. Furthermore, the method is extended to include an additional channel describing the exchange of particles between the environment and the system, and the resulting equations are used to analyze a system with both dissipation and particle exchange. An example shows that the collapse of a system initially in a coherent state is primarily due to a two-step process involving simultaneous emission and absorption of particles.

Using the Tamm-Danielsson formalism and the Fermi golden rule, the effect of nanostructured aluminum on the absorption in thin-film silicon solar cells was examined. Two specific silicon samples, with varying thicknesses of 1.5 $\mu$m and 1.0 $\mu$m, were subjected to three diverse aluminum (AL) layer thicknesses and three varied aluminum (AL) nanoparticle diameters. For each of the 12 samples, the enhancement of absorption coefficient $\kappa$ was calculated and plotted against the wavelength. Our results indicate that the absorption coefficient $\kappa$ is significantly influenced by the aluminum (AL) nanoparticle diameter and AL layer thickness. Moreover, the system's resonance frequency was found to be sensitive to the varying dimensions of the aluminum (AL) nanoparticle.

We introduce a restricted family of programming languages, which encompass a counting-based logic programming language, a counting-based procedural programming language, and a novel counting-free language. In this context, the counting-free language is capable of efficiently calculating exact counts for sets of basic data structures such as numbers, but it achieves this by employing a query resolution process that is inherently inefficient. It is demonstrated that these languages collectively capture a broad class of deterministic logic programs that can be evaluated in polynomial time, specifically within PTIME. Notably, the counting-based logic and procedural programming languages represent the fundamental elements of this collection, and the counting-free language can be viewed as an extension of the procedural programming language in a broader sense.

Deep learning has become increasingly popular in vision-related fields, particularly in video analysis. However, the significant computational cost associated with processing large volumes of video data has hindered the widespread adoption of deep learning in real-time video analysis. In an effort to mitigate this issue, this study presents a co-design approach that optimizes algorithmic and hardware development to minimize power consumption. By leveraging the Hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition of long-term memory networks, our solution achieves a notable 7.5x reduction in model parameters and 1.4x decrease in power consumption compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, our solution is capable of maintaining its accuracy even when faced with reduced bit depth, resulting in a power savings of up to 2x during execution.

The MAVLink protocol, used by the widely adopted ARDUPILOT and PX4 flight control softwares, enables communication between drones and ground control. Unfortunately, its lack of modern security features leaves it vulnerable to attacks. This paper proposes a solution to address the security concerns, suggesting the development of a secure MAVLink implementation, specifically designed for use within the BeagleBone Black's Linux-based system. This system would provide an additional security layer for controllers and drones, offering an additional defense mechanism against potential attacks.

We introduce a dynamic parallel platform for large-scale structural dynamics simulations, aiming to solve complex problems requiring both spatial and temporal precision.  The framework is structured as a distributed graph where vertices represent nodes and edges signify communication.  Each node solves a partial problem, exchanging data with neighboring nodes via custom, user-defined interactions.  Our goal is to accurately simulate the dynamic behavior of a system, without imposing limitations on problem size or complexity.  The challenge is to ensure the solution's accuracy at each step, given the potential for numerical issues arising from the simulation's complexity and time-step size.  To address this, we employ a novel approach, combining a distributed graph structure and adaptive step-size control to produce high-quality simulations.

The Newman-Penrose scalar perturbation formalism, based on asymptotically smooth spacetime metrics, has been widely used to analyze gravitational wave behavior and Teukolsky equations since the 1960s.  We demonstrate that this formalism can be equivalently defined within the realm of twistor theory, utilizing domain walls and holomorphic variables in gauge theory.  Furthermore, this alternative understanding provides a natural framework for exploring the Cauchy problem in mathematical physics.

Muons are high-energy particles that penetrate Earth's dense material easily and can cover significant distances at low angles of approach. Researchers are utilizing muons as sensitive sensors to study the internal structure of the Earth from above its surface. A major research focus revolves around detecting muons created when high-energy cosmic rays collide with the atmosphere, a phenomenon that has gained significant attention over the past decade. A major challenge lies in accurately identifying and differentiating muons from background cosmic ray events, and this task becomes even more complex in subterranean detection systems. A new muon sensor, engineered over an extended period using the most advanced technology available, is presented here in an effort to enhance the accuracy of muon tracking and detection. This detector is designed to integrate seamlessly into an underground system and can help researchers detect and map underground air pockets, voids, and other cavities with greater precision.

Internal logic terms are often represented as strings of symbols, each carrying a specific meaning. Different meanings can be indicated by different labels or by distinct symbols. Research has shown that using distinct symbols can result in better performance, but it requires understanding of the underlying semantics of the symbols.

This paper explores this issue by comparing performance in two languages - Lisp-like and C-like syntax - when using both symbol-based and label-based representation. Key findings are that (1) one language performs better than the other, (2) using distinct symbols yields better results, and (3) the improvement in performance is independent of the used language.

This research explores how modified temperature-dependent Maxwell's equations, derived from the $U(1)$ Yang-Mills-Higgs model, impact the propagation of charged particles and resultant vacuum Cherenkov radiation. A comprehensive analysis is conducted on the particles' transport behavior and radiation emission process through solutions of the corresponding Boltzmann equation and a transport equation derived from the Vlasov equation. Our findings demonstrate that the emission of radiation is significantly influenced by thermal effects at high temperatures, even showing a reversal in direction below a critical temperature, in contrast to the prevailing understanding at absolute zero.

This study presents a groundbreaking approach to tracking predictions made by individuals during natural speech, which diverge from the actual outcome, known as verbal predictions. Unlike previous studies, our work focuses on the fine-tuning of neural language models to simulate human performance, allowing us to analyze and interpret the results of verbal prediction errors. Our analysis reveals that the models' behavior is influenced by their training data and that their sensitivity to these data properties matches patterns observed in human behavior, which can be applied to better comprehend verbal prediction inaccuracies.

A straightforward way to identify the three-dimensional structure of an object from a single two-dimensional image is to determine its position from its rotation. This is a relatively easy task, especially when observing objects that can be identified as three-dimensional 'turntables' through a series of related views. However, this issue becomes more complex when analyzing images of unknown objects that cannot be linked in this way. A new approach to overcome this problem involves a 'learning by observation' method that enables a model to recognize a reliable three-dimensional shape from an image of an object that has been confirmed by user interaction. This method was tested using a large dataset of objects and showed a significant improvement in accuracy compared to previous methods, as demonstrated by the results on a large dataset of objects and a smaller set of objects.

In a superconducting nanowire with a magnetic field applied, managing Andreev bound states is crucial for controlling quantum interference effects in superconductors. Our research shows that combining a magnetic field with an electrostatic gate allows precise control of the interference effects through a novel device design. We demonstrate how the magnetic field and gate work together to manage these states in our nanowire, which leads to optimal suppression of a type of interference known as crossed Andreev reflection. Furthermore, our findings indicate that suppressing this interference enables a significant reduction of a different type of leakage event called elastic co-tunneling.

In this work, the author proposes a simplified model for particle acceleration in magnetic reconnection that incorporates an ad hoc pitch-angle scattering mechanism. This model involves a transport equation with anisotropic diffusion, whose solutions can be accurately matched to the outcomes of two- and three-dimensional simulations of magnetic reconnection. The proposed model successfully replicates key characteristics of the simulated particles' behavior, including their speed distribution, magnetic moment evolution, and the formation of a suprathermal tail. Importantly, the model's performance is significantly improved when it assumes a non-uniform scattering mechanism, as evidenced by its ability to accurately predict the simulated particles' speed distributions. This simplification is particularly advantageous because it facilitates the analytical treatment of complex phenomena like magnetic reconnection, where detailed comparisons with simulations are essential.

Within the framework of linearly-realised expanded scalar sectors, our analysis reveals that the process of $e^+e^- \to Zh$ serves as a particularly sensitive means of detection, given its superior sensitivity relative to LHC searches for di-photon decays of the heavy CP-even Higgs boson $H$. This outcome is largely attributed to the substantial production of $H$ via the process $e^+e^- \to HZZ$ in colliders featuring polarized beams. Furthermore, our study extends the current analysis to include a two-Higgs-doublet model with a charged field $H^\pm$.
A set normed by the combined numerical radius is shown to have a subdifferential that is comprised of matrices with rank one or zero.

A new monetary incentive mechanism for peer-to-peer learning has been introduced, allowing for more efficient model training through a unique system of experience points and rewards. This mechanism enables participants to earn and exchange virtual experience tokens, used to train models from peer-to-peer learning platforms. The proposed mechanism addresses a crucial gap in existing learning frameworks, providing a monetary incentive scheme for data scientists while safeguarding sensitive information. Additionally, our solution offers secure and efficient data protection mechanisms, ensuring the confidentiality of sensitive data and financial transactions, while maintaining the integrity of the learning process.

In stochastic systems, random variables and functions can be analyzed using the concept of stochastic mappings, which are functions mapping probability distributions to others. These stochastic mappings are prominent in stochastic fields and have significant applications in stochastics and other fields. This study aims to introduce a novel approach for stochastic mappings, which utilizes the correlation between different probability distributions. This method provides a basis for determining the correlation between stochastic mappings and has far-reaching implications for understanding stochastic systems. We demonstrate the practical implications of stochastic mappings, which are referred to as allocation fields, and have numerous applications in modeling and analysis of complex stochastic systems. This study's approach is illustrated through examples and case studies and is expected to have significant applications in various fields.

Our investigation into the high-pressure mixture He-H2-O2, with He, H2, and O2 as its constituents, reveals a distinct photochemical reaction zone formed through the unconfined laser-induced combustion (ULIC) process. This reaction zone exhibits characteristics of a stationary, shock-driven combustion interface, accompanied by a notable pressure and temperature gradient. The O2 consumption in the process indicates the formation of water, while the H2 and He within the reaction zone experience significant pressure decrease due to thermal and adiabatic effects. The resulting combustion produces water vapor, contributing to the growth of the photochemical zone, thereby indicating the occurrence of a dynamic reaction process. The reaction zone's growth is influenced by the initial pressure, with a notable increase observed from 10 to 30 bar, while the development of water vapor and pressure within the reaction zone follows a power-law growth, specifically a $ \propto t^2$ rate.

In this study, a boundary-sensitive segmentation network is created to effectively identify object boundaries. The proposed network is built upon a novel framework that integrates boundary information into both the encoder and decoder. The network's efficiency and accuracy are validated by experimental results on multiple datasets, and its source code is made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhubongyu/Boundary-Net.

This research introduces an innovative system for collaborative work between vehicles equipped with communication and control capabilities, with the goal of developing a driver-assistance application for lane-change operations.  The system is designed to manage a network of cooperating vehicles to provide the driver with guidance on safe lane-change execution, utilizing communication standards compliant with ADAS MC between vehicles and display information to the driver through various warning systems.

In this study, we investigate the statistical characteristics of non-interacting, weakly active particles that move within various two- and three-dimensional geometries. Our research reveals that, in unconfined environments, these particles adopt distinct velocity distributions that, depending on the spatial dimension, are characterized by Gaussian, exponential, or square-root tails. Furthermore, we observe that confinement significantly impacts the velocity distribution of active particles. Specifically, in two-dimensional geometries, confinement leads to a transition from a Gaussian distribution to a power-law tail, whereas in three-dimensional geometologies, confinement gives rise to a distinct transition from exponential to Gaussian-like distributions. Our findings are supported by simulations of active particles in various geometries and provide new insights into the velocity distribution of confined active particles.

In a model based on the Dicke's atom-field Hamiltonian, we study the resonator's transmission coefficient when driven by a classical field near its resonance frequency, which exhibits superradiant scattering. By introducing atom-field coupling variations based on the atom's energy levels, we establish a connection to random matrix theory and examine the two-level scenario. As the number of atoms increases, we observe that the resonance peak's width is primarily influenced by the linear combination of the atom-field coupling strength and the resonance frequency, which is characteristic of Siegert levels. Specifically, we find that the resonator's transmission coefficient is proportional to the square of the number of atoms and exhibits a Siegert level with a corresponding width at large $N$. In contrast, for the case of many energy levels, we derive a universal expression for the resonant transmission probability which scales as the square of the number of levels and exhibits Siegert behavior.

Observations of the Si IV 1398 Angstrom double-peak profiles, recorded by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly on the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph, have revealed sub-second frequency fluctuations in a 2008 solar flare. Specifically, the intensity ratios between the two peaks of the Si IV profiles experienced rapid oscillations of around 30% in under one second. Notably, the red peak tended to be more prominent than the blue peak throughout the flare event. However, the relative intensities of the peaks reverted to their typical configurations during a brief period of reduced flare activity.

We investigate the interplay between the CP violation arising from quantum dynamics and the origin of CP violation, particularly in relation to fundamental axion models. We find that the quantum dynamics of $1/N$ corrections to the QCD partition function, typically used to justify the strong CP problem, are not independent of fundamental axion models, but rather rely on the same underlying CP violation. This implies that resolving the strong CP problem in fundamental axion models will simultaneously address the apparent CP violation in the QCD partition function. We also examine the implications of this connection for the constraints on the axion mass and the direction of the axion vacuum's winding, with the constraint on the axion mass being determined by the fine-tuning of the QCD partition function.

The impact of a key physical process, termed quasi-equilibrium in realistic simulations, significantly affects the point at which irradiated materials cease to form diffraction patterns. This quasi-equilibrium is influenced by the unique interactions between ion-induced effects and material properties, resulting in varying levels of this equilibrium in different materials. As a result, materials with high quasi-equilibrium are more suitable for practical purposes like lithography. Furthermore, realistic simulations demonstrate that this equilibrium can be defined by a single parameter, thereby simplifying the analysis and prediction of system behavior.

In competitive environments, such as game programming, cheating is often addressed by verifying the authenticity of source code, which is a straightforward measure, although it may limit collaboration between developers due to increased control over code execution. In order to facilitate collaboration while preventing cheating, we propose a novel approach that allows the use of open-source code libraries while preventing unauthorized execution of critical parts of the code, while still enabling the execution of the rest of the program. In this paper, we present an implementation of the routing method in C#, demonstrating its application in a game setting where a developer compiles their code into two separate files: a library and a main program. The library contains sensitive code that is executed under runtime environment control, whereas the main program contains controlled code that is executed through the routing method, thereby requiring no additional developer input to run.

In the past, Strauch and Yang have studied the convergence of certain automorphic Dirichlet sums, focusing on the representation theory aspects, but leaving some cases incomplete. This paper builds on Yang's work, exploring a broader category of sums, and provides a comprehensive solution, utilizing previously established results by the author.
We establish that in groups with fast growth, units form a metric near-subgroup if and only if the group's isomorphism type is represented by a group with a polynomially bounded word length spectrum.

In this paper, we propose a groundbreaking approach to calculate the likelihood of log-concave probability density functions. Our system features a unique, highly interconnected structure that processes data in a global manner, with a significant emphasis on maintaining log-concavity. This architecture generates high-quality estimates by optimizing the distribution in a way that minimizes the negative log-likelihood. Our system's global structure allows us to derive precise formulas for the factors that influence the likelihood, which we can then optimize using advanced techniques. We have developed a highly efficient optimization method that leverages the factors and is guaranteed to converge to a global optimum. Our approach is capable of handling large datasets and diverse distribution families, including the normal, t and Cauchy. We have conducted extensive tests to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and have shown that it outperforms existing popular algorithms.

Research into the static configuration space of granular materials has been limited by the lack of computational methods that can efficiently explore and map this space. A unified framework for analyzing various types of granular materials is needed to better understand the interplay between mechanical properties and packing structure, particularly in terms of macroscopic behavior. This study proposes a novel Monte Carlo sampling approach based on the Wang-Landau algorithm, enabling the calculation of entropy in response to external forces. By applying this method, we successfully calculated entropy for a granular assembly subject to arching and jamming conditions, achieving a 10-fold increase in efficiency compared to existing approaches. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of granular materials, with our results demonstrating the versatility and efficiency of this method in analyzing granular materials, particularly those encountered in civil engineering applications.

We present a graph-based framework for the Adventurer-Manager game, a game theory framework that models a competitive relationship between a manager and adventurer. Their interactions are governed by a formula that calculates the value of their shared resources, taking into consideration the manager's strategy and the adventurer's strategy. We investigate the properties of the Adventurer-Manager game on specific types of graphs, such as bipartite graphs, and observe that certain generalizations of the game yield certain conclusions. We also demonstrate that the Adventurer-Manager game on trees lacks optimal strategies for the adventurer, and we outline a future research direction, while providing initial results for more complex graphs like planar graphs.

We examine a stochastic process, known as a Gaussian process, and derive exact analytical expressions for its spectral power-spectral distribution at two distinct frequency frequencies. These expressions reveal a relationship between the process' spectral distributions at these frequencies, demonstrating how the distribution at a higher frequency is obtained from the lower frequency through convolution with a Gaussian weight function. This weight function is characterized by a standard deviation that is inversely proportional to that same higher frequency. Furthermore, we establish a mapping between the autocorrelation function of this process at its lowest frequency and the process's spectral power-spectral distribution at its higher frequency, a relationship that holds regardless of the nature of the Gaussian weight function's standard deviation.

We investigate static solutions of the Broer-Kaufl model with a broad range of parameters, focusing on a family of parameter values that give rise to a reduced equation. Utilizing the Darboux transformation, we derive a new family of static solutions with diverse properties, including periodicity, large amplitude, and non-monotonic behavior. Additionally, an implicit integration technique is used to address the first-order dynamics associated with the Broer-Kaufl system, yielding static solution sequences that rectify the original system's defects.

This study focuses on a specific type of incompressible Euler flow that is bounded within a bounded area and possesses Lebesgue boundedness in both space and time. Under these conditions, it is proven that even with the initial conditions having vanishing circulation, the resulting flow still preserves energy. The findings presented here improve upon a previously established result by the first author in 2013. The key contribution of this paper is attributed to a rigorous integration-by-parts argument, along with a concept based on the initial vorticity's temporal integration that determines the spatial alignment of the velocity field.

The Virtual Reality industry is projected to experience rapid growth in the near future, with a projected increase in revenue to $62 billion by 2030, up from $13.9 billion in 2020. This growth is largely driven by advancements in VR/AR technology, with a focus on more realistic and immersive experiences. However, to further enhance user engagement, a novel area of research is needed, involving the concept of making the real world appear fake. The Virtual Reality Universal Project (VIRUP) aims to tackle this challenge by creating an integrated framework that brings together computer vision, augmented reality, and virtual reality to modify the physical environment. Specifically, VIRUP will develop a system to alter the appearance of a self-driving car's surroundings by manipulating its camera inputs. Key objectives of VIRUP include creating a realistic digital representation of the environment, modifying the digital view to make it appear as if the real world is part of a virtual or augmented reality. Key technical challenges that VIRUP seeks to address include: (i) developing a robust method for creating photorealistic 3D reconstructions of the environment, (ii) modifying the digital view in a way that maintains the user's perception of continuity, and (iii) ensuring that the modified digital view does not cause disorientation or alter the user's perception of depth. The key performance metrics for evaluating VIRUP are: (i) the similarity between the real-world and digital views; (ii) the user's perception of the environment

This paper describes the development of Data Bricks, an interactive system that helps children understand data, by utilizing both visualization and manipulation of objects. Our primary objective was to determine whether young users can leverage this system to acquire basic data understanding skills and comprehend basic queries. In order to evaluate the system's effectiveness, a series of experiments were conducted with a group of sixty children between the ages of 8-12. These children were divided into three distinct groups and instructed using three distinct approaches. The first group received traditional training, while the other two groups learned through either hands-on Data Bricks training or a video-based training. Our findings indicate that children who received both hands-on and video training demonstrated significant improvement in their data understanding skills in comparison to those who received traditional training. Interestingly, children who received hands-on training exhibited superior performance in data comprehension, while those who received video training excelled in query-related skills. Our research also uncovered that children who were more familiar with computers demonstrated improved data manipulation skills, but that this proficiency did not translate to data visualization skills.

The software defined networking technology offers a range of benefits, both for end users and data centers. To make the most of SDN, the development of efficient and innovative algorithms for packet data transfer is essential. SDDM is a novel approach that enables SDDN to function by converting packet data into a more compact format, minimizing the time it takes to access and retrieve data in the data-path. This is achieved through the strategic placement of SDDM engines, which optimize the use of on-chip memory. This research focuses on the design and optimization of a novel SDDM core that takes advantage of the underlying on-chip network. This core is specifically designed to minimize data-path functions, using a combination of advanced mathematical algorithms and circuit design. The design of the SDDM core uses a hybrid approach that takes into account the specific requirements of the application, using a combination of linear and non-linear functions to achieve optimal performance. The resulting SDDM core is significantly smaller and more efficient than traditional data-path architectures. The design process is further optimized by using a combination of algorithms and circuit approximations to minimize the complexity of the SDDM core. The resulting design is then implemented and tested using a cutting-edge FPGA platform, demonstrating a substantial reduction in area and improvements in latency and energy efficiency. The results show that the SDDM core achieves a 70% reduction in area, 20% reduction in latency, and 30% reduction in energy consumption compared to traditional data-path

In many practical settings, datasets exhibit inherent relationships, structured in a graph format resulting from connections between interconnected entities. For instance, a graph of social interactions can be created based on the connections between individuals, a graph of product associations based on the items within an e-commerce platform, or a graph of gene interactions based on the study of biological processes. These relationships can be leveraged to learn a disentangled feature representation capable of capturing the underlying structure of the data. However, our research reveals that disentanglement is not always beneficial and, in fact, can lead to a loss of valuable information when applied naively. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach to learning weakly untangled representations that balance the preservation of information with the benefits of disentanglement. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this approach over existing state-of-the-art techniques, showcasing its ability to yield better performance on complex real-world datasets.

The efficiency of energy collection by an oscillating blade can be significantly affected by the wake's characteristics that result from the preceding blade's motion. This study investigates the intricate relationship between the wake formed by the preceding blade and its impact on the following blade by analyzing various patterns of motion. It was discovered that a sudden change in angle between the blades has a more substantial impact on the wake than a sudden change in speed. Furthermore, it was observed that a larger second blade experiences a weaker wake than a smaller one, suggesting that there are opportunities to enhance energy collection efficiency. This study provides valuable insights for designing optimal tandem blade arrangements for practical applications.

We examine the real-time behavior of hadron spectral functions at various temperatures, obtained from lattice QCD simulations, by applying a Bayesian model that considers different thermal states. The spectral functions are represented as a mixture of overlapping patterns generated by hadrons, which form our model's parameters. The function's real-time evolution is analyzed by varying the relative intensity of these patterns, representing different hadron resonances. The outcome reveals that the lattice results primarily indicate the presence of quark plasmas. The uncertainty in the thermal energy distribution is found to significantly influence the spectral signal's real-time behavior. The model also shows that the lattice data primarily attribute the continuum real-time behavior to a combination of baryon and meson resonances. The findings from this study support the use of this Bayesian approach in interpreting lattice data.

In quantum systems, electron tunneling processes often occur with the spins being either uninvolved or explicitly involved. Our investigation focuses on the electron tunneling process between a mobile electron and a localized electron in two-dimensional structures. In our research, we discovered that the electron tunneling process, which typically involves spinless tunneling, can become the primary mechanism when the energy barrier is sufficiently low. In this context, we observed a decrease in the superconducting order parameter, which is influenced by the spin flip during the electron tunneling process. Our findings suggest that the electron tunneling process, which involves spin, becomes the dominant mechanism when the energy barrier is sufficiently low. In addition, we found that the electron tunneling process, which involves spin, can lead to an increase in the critical temperature of the superconductor, which is in line with theoretical predictions.

In the field of drug discovery, identifying potential candidates from a vast library of molecular structures is a key objective. A major challenge is finding a balance between a molecule's efficacy in targeting specific disease receptors and its stability in terms of energy. A solution to this issue can be achieved through the use of generative models, which can quickly generate new molecules that meet certain requirements. Nevertheless, current models are limited in their ability to predict energy-related properties of molecules. We have developed a generative model, which we call the Energy-driven Generative Model, and have used it to create a dataset of simulated molecular structures. This dataset was then utilized to train a more advanced generative model, which we call the Energy-driven Generative Model with Transformer. When put to the test, our Energy-driven Generative Model with Transformer outperformed the other models examined by a significant margin. Furthermore, our Energy-driven Generative Model with Transformer is the first model of its kind to simultaneously predict energy-related properties of molecules. This breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize the field of drug discovery by enabling the rapid design of new molecules with a high degree of accuracy.

Token-based digital advertising platforms utilize a unique approach, 
focusing on interaction rather than simply displaying ads based on cost.
These types of ads often appear in news content or social media posts.
Our analysis involves creating a network model to represent user interactions,
using tokens to track user connections to ad content.
By examining the geometric structure of our network, we hope to gain insights
into user engagement and inform the design of future interactive ad schemes.
Our study was conducted using data from two distinct advertising systems,
Energetic Machines, Inc. and The New York Times Company.

The Large Magellanic Cloud's (LMC) outer regions, specifically the outer ring and the south-eastern tail, are subject to a unique environment. Located between the LMC and the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), they have been affected by the SMC's gravitational pull. This study examines the motion of stars in these areas, using precise parallax measurements from Gaia, and compares them to the motion of stars in other regions. The results indicate that stars in the outer LMC and the SMC move more slowly than those in the central areas, with the former areas having higher probabilities of being associated with the SMC. The study also finds that the motion of stars in the outer ring is consistent with the motion of stars in the outer tail, both of which are expected to be tidally stripped from the central disk. The motion of stars in the outer regions is expected to be influenced by the SMC's gravitational pull, with the study concluding that the motion of stars in the outer ring and tail is likely to be similar to that of stars in the outer SMC.
